The practices and tools that govern how you move code and configurations from development through testing to production. If testing validates, "Does this work locally?" then ALM answers, "Can we deploy this safely and track what changed?" In traditional software, ALM has been around for decades, but agentic systems with agents, connectors, custom tools, and AI models, that introduces new complexity.

[06:48] Real-world scenario number two, the model swap with zero downtime. So, let's say you have a customer service agent running GPT-4 in production. It works well, but it's expensive, $3 per user per day. Your team trained a fine-tuned GPT-3.5 model that's 70% as capable, but it costs 50 cents per user per day.

[07:14] You want to switch to the new model, but you need zero downtime. Your agent serves 50,000 daily users. Here's where blue/green deployment comes in. You create a blue environment running the original GPT-4. This is production handling all the real traffic. You create a green environment running the new fine-tuned GPT-3.5. This is idle, not receiving traffic. You run E2E test in green, you validate quality, you run AB test with 5% of the real traffic. If green performs well, you flip the switch, all traffic goes to green. If something goes wrong, you flip back to blue instantly. No downtime.

[07:57] This is production deployment done right. Here's real-world scenario number three, the rollback scenario. An agent you deployed yesterday is hallucinating answers to 8% of queries, the normal's like 0.05%. Something about the deployed version is broken, but you're not sure what. With ALM and versioning, here's what happens. You detect the issue through monitoring, that 8% hallucination rate spike. You immediately roll back to the previous stable version in production.

[08:30] Users are restored to the normal behavior within minutes. Now you have time to investigate what went wrong in the newer version. When you understand the problem, you fix it in dev, and then you retest and redeploy. Without ALM, without versioning and rollback capability, you're stuck. You have a broken agent and no clear way to revert. Now, once you've rolled back, you investigate. Compare the broken version against the stable one. Find the root cause, maybe an incomplete grounding data update. Fix it in dev, retest, and redeploy properly. Now, let's talk about versioning strategy. Semantic versioning is common.

[09:11] Major.minor.patch. So, the major means a breaking change, the agent behavior is significantly different. Minor is a new feature or capability that is backward compatible. And patch is a bug fix, no new features. So, example 2.1.5, version two, that's a major, the second major release.

[09:36] Version one, that's your minor. The first minor feature set that was added. And then five, that's your patch. That's the fifth bug fix on this major minor combination. When you tag a version in Co-pilot Studio or Foundry, you document what changed. This is your change log. Additionally, you can tag versions with environment information like version 2.1.5-prod deployed to production on March 15th.

[10:07] Version 2.1.4-staging in staging. Now for models specifically, each version in the Foundry registry should include richer metadata like the training date and the data sources, accuracy and fairness metrics, known limitations, who trained it, and who approved it for deployment. If a user reports an issue with a specific model version, you can pull it from the registry, review the metadata, and compare with other versions to isolate the problem. Without this metadata, you're just guessing.

[10:45] Now let's talk about managing connectors and flows. Custom connectors are part of your Agentry system. They connect your agent to external APIs. In Power Platform, connectors are versioned. When you change a connector like a new endpoint or new authentication, you create a version. Flows that use those connectors reference specific versions.

[11:11] If you update a connector version, all flows are notified. You test them, and you update them, and you deploy them. Now here's the critical part. If a flow uses connector version 1.2 and you release connector version 2.0, that means breaking change, that flow doesn't automatically break. It still uses 1.2 until you explicitly update it. Now, governance gates formalize this. A developer submits a change request describing what, why, and the risk, and a rollback plan. The change review board evaluates the strategy alignment, security, compliance, and the business value. They approve, reject, or approve with conditions. After deployment, you monitor KPIs for 30 minutes, check user

[12:01] satisfaction, cost impact, any issues. Document your lessons learned. Governance isn't bureaucracy. It's risk management. And finally, models in Foundry. Foundry has a model registry. Every time you fine-tune or train a new model version, you register it. You can deploy different versions to different environments. You can AB test versions with real traffic.

[12:28] And you can quickly roll back if a version underperforms. The Foundry registry is the single source of truth for which model version is deployed where. Here's a real decision. Version 1.1.0 has 94% accuracy at 10 cents per inference. Version 1.2 has a 96% accuracy at 12 cents.

[12:55] That's a 2% accuracy gain with a 20% cost increase. In in many domains, the answer is yes. We want the 20% cost because accuracy affects user trust. Models don't live in isolation. They need data, and data needs to be tracked and governed. That brings us to data lineage and Microsoft Purview. Your agent's grounding data comes from somewhere.

[13:23] SharePoint, a database, external APIs, PDFs. When the agent fails or gives wrong answers, you need to trace the problem back. Where did this data come from? Is it fresh? Is it accurate? Who has access to it? Microsoft Purview data catalog answers these questions. It tracks data sources. Where does the data live? Data lineage. How does data flow from one source to the agent?

[13:52] And then data quality. Is the data validated and current? Data classifications. Is it PII, confidential, or public? And data governance. Who has access? Who can modify it? Here's an example lineage flow. So, your HR database, the master source, syncs daily to SharePoint. SharePoint gets indexed every 6 hours into Azure AI search. The agent retrieves from that index for context, passes it to the model, and the model generates output.

[14:29] If the agent gives wrong HR advice, you investigate using Purview. Is the index data stale? Did the SharePoint sync fail? Are there quality issues in the source data? The root cause might be the SharePoint sync failed yesterday, so the agent has old data. Fix the sync, refresh the index, and accuracy improves. Data quality gates add another layer of protection.

[14:55] Before data is used for training or grounding, automated checks run. Were all the required fields populated? Are values in their expected ranges? Are there duplicates? Is the data balanced across classes? If any gate fails, the data is quarantined and an alert is sent. No bad data reaches the model. So, here's a real-world scenario where a data quality gate catches bad training data.

[15:23] You're training a new version of a loan approval model. Your training data is 100,000 historical loan applications. A data engineer loads the training data, but a bug in the extract process corrupts 5% of the records. Without data quality gates, the model trains on corrupted data and accuracy drops. You deploy it, users get bad predictions, you discover the problem weeks later through complaints and audits.

[15:51] With data quality gates, the automated checks catch the corrupted values. The training halts, an alert fires, the data engineer fixes the extract query, reloads the data, the checks pass, and the trading data proceeds. A 2-hour delay that prevents a bad model from reaching production. What does the AB 100 expect for ALM? Well, strong answers include separate environments, semantic versioning with metadata, CICD pipelines with automated testing, manual approval gates like code review and change board, rollback capability using blue-green or version snapshots, version tracking for agents, connectors, and models, data lineage with purview and audit trail showing who changed what, when,

[16:43] and why. Weak answers are single environment where testing and production are the same. There's no versioning. You do manual deployments with no approval agents, no rollback capability, only agents versioned while connectors and models are ignored, and no audit trail. If an exam says an agent update broke production, walk through your ALM strategy. Here's how a strong answer sounds. We have separate environments.

[17:13] Every change goes through CICD with auto test, code reviews, change board approval, and staging deployment. When the break happened, monitoring detected the spike in seconds. We rolled back instantly using blue/green. Downtime was under 30 seconds. We compared the broken version to the previous stable version, found what changed, fixed it in dev, retested, and redeployed through the full pipeline again.

[17:43] That's exam-level thinking. So, here's your key takeaways. One, version everything: agents, connectors, models, flows, with metadata tracking and who changed what and when. Two, govern data with purview lineage tracking and quality gates. Bad data in means bad models out. Three, enforce separate environments: a dev environment, test environment, staging, and then production. Never test in production.

[18:13] Four, automate with CI/CD using GitHub Actions or Azure DevOps for consistent, auditable deployments. Five, establish governance gates. Code review plus change board plus compliance review. Six, design for rollback. Blue/green deployments and version snapshots so you can revert instantly.
